title: Feedback and System Status
editorial_note: Automated dialogue draft from the revised lesson. Review spoken wording and meaning before publishing.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Today we're talking about Feedback and System Status. By the end, you'll know why this matters, how to use it, and what to notice in a real product.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What is the problem we are trying to understand?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Feedforward helps people predict what an action will do. Feedback helps them interpret what happened. System status makes current progress, state, and uncertainty visible. Together they reduce anxiety, errors, and repeated actions.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Why does that happen?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Match feedback to consequence and latency. Immediate reversible actions may need subtle acknowledgement; high-stakes or delayed actions need durable, specific confirmation. Loading states should explain progress or waiting rather than merely animate. Preserve the evidence of completion when a person may need it later.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Close the loop between action and reliable state
turns.text: What changes when we look at close the loop between action and reliable state?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Feedback acknowledges an interaction; system status explains the state that now exists. A button press animation can show that input was received, but it cannot prove that a clinic accepted a transfer. Useful feedback is proportionate to latency and consequence, tied to the affected object, and clear about whether work is local, transmitted, processed, or complete.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The team tests quick, delayed, partial, duplicated, and failed operations, plus background completion after the user leaves. It measures double submission, false belief, recovery, and support demand. The next lesson’s hierarchy work determines which status deserves attention without allowing urgency styling to outrun truth.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at transfer example: file upload?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: An upload can be selected, transferred, scanned, processed, and published. Showing 100% after bytes reach the server may falsely imply availability. A good status model distinguishes phases, permits safe cancellation where possible, and explains what happens if processing continues in the background.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Match feedback to time and consequence
turns.text: What changes when we look at match feedback to time and consequence?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Immediate actions need immediate acknowledgement. Longer work needs progress, meaningful stages, expectation, and a way to leave or cancel. Completion needs a clear outcome and next step. Errors need cause where useful, preserved effort, and recovery. Feedback should exist visually and programmatically without depending on colour or animation alone.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Avoid false precision and theatrical loading. If duration is unknown, communicate activity and what the person can do. Distinguish queued, processing, completed, failed, and partially completed states. For consequential operations, provide an inspectable history and idempotent behaviour so retries do not duplicate action.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Make status durable, truthful, and actionable
turns.text: What changes when we look at make status durable, truthful, and actionable?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Feedback uses multiple channels without multiplying contradiction: visible text, focus movement, live-region announcement, email or message, and support state all derive from the same source model. Motion or colour can reinforce a change but cannot carry it alone. Repeated notifications are governed so urgency remains meaningful.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Where does the harder design decision appear?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Status design depends on real system observability. If the product cannot tell whether a payment succeeded, language alone cannot create trustworthy feedback.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should we look at more closely?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Feedback has a lifecycle. Before action, feedforward lets a person predict the consequence. During action, status indicates that work is accepted, pending, or blocked. After action, confirmation records what happened and what remains.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: For asynchronous or high-consequence work, a temporary toast is not enough: people may need a durable receipt, history entry, status page, notification, or clear escalation path.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Design for uncertainty honestly. A progress indicator should not pretend to know an exact remaining time when the system cannot. Explain whether a person can leave, retry, cancel, or safely take another action. Distinguish local interface acknowledgement from successful service completion, especially when a payment, upload, approval, or sync continues in the background.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Failure modes to watch

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: False completion: an interface confirms before the underlying service has finished. Silent latency: a person cannot tell whether to wait, retry, or seek help. Ephemeral evidence: confirmation disappears before it can support later verification. Same feedback for every consequence: a low-risk toggle and an irreversible transfer receive equally weak acknowledgement.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can we see that in a concrete product situation?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: After pressing “Pay,” a button becomes disabled and nothing else changes. The person does not know whether the payment is processing, failed, duplicated, or complete.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: How does this connect to what we have already learned?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Worked example A transfer flow first says “Done” when the request is queued. Customers assume money arrived and repeat the action. The redesign distinguishes submitted, processing, completed, and failed, shows recipient and amount, prevents duplicate submission, and provides a traceable reference. Status is available to screen readers and support staff.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Better feedback changed behaviour because it represented the real service state rather than the interface event. Forms collect input. Feedback closes the loop between action and outcome. lesson 47 makes the visual hierarchy of that loop legible at a glance.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should I notice the next time I use a product?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Watch a loading or confirmation state. What information would reduce uncertainty about progress, outcome, or next action?
